Executive Summary: PathSnap addresses the high-dimensional offline map-matching challenge: reconstructing true continuous road trajectories from sparse, noisy GPS coordinates over dense road graph networks. By combining metric UTM KD-tree spatial projection, kinematic feature engineering, a gradient-boosted ensemble candidate scorer, and a distance-aware Hidden Markov Model (HMM) Viterbi decoder, our system achieves 98.1% route continuity and sub-second inference latency across student evaluation trips.

1. Dataset Understanding & Exploratory Data Analysis

The PathSnap dataset consists of 90 distinct vehicle trips partitioned into 80 training trips and 10 held-out student test trips, totaling 227,577 GPS observations. Each trip forms an independent spatial subgraph defined by four core files:

  • <id>.track: Temporal sequence of raw GPS pings ([longitude, latitude, timestamp]).
  • <id>.nodes: Spatial coordinates of street junctions and geometry vertices (~22,490 nodes/trip).
  • <id>.arcs: Directed graph edges representing drivable segments and one-way streets (~45,132 arcs/trip).
  • <id>.route: Ground-truth sequential arc indices traversed by the vehicle.

Key Exploratory Findings & Preprocessing Strategy

1. GPS Sensor Drift & Spatial Projection: Analysis revealed a median GPS drift of 4.30m from the true road centerline, with 99.9% within 25.0m and extreme anomalies reaching 27.2m. Coordinates were transformed from WGS84 to metric UTM Zone 43N (EPSG:32643) using pyproj. A spatial index using scipy.spatial.cKDTree with a 75.0m search radius and 3-nearest-neighbor fallback was established to guarantee candidate segment retrieval.

2. Parallel Road Ambiguity: When vehicles traverse parallel highways, frontage roads, or intersections, perpendicular Euclidean distance alone is ambiguous (delta < 2m). We engineered bearing_alignment_deg (|θGPS - θSegment|). This angular divergence (>90° for cross-streets/parallel lanes) provides critical discriminative signal.

3. Sampling Irregularities: While 94.32% of GPS pings were sampled at exactly 1.0s intervals, we identified 3,075 temporal gaps >2s caused by satellite obstruction. Kinematic speeds (point_speed_mps) and road speed limit proxies were derived to penalize physically impossible transitions.

Figure 1: Exploratory analysis showing observation counts, trip duration distribution, sampling time deltas, and speed distributions.

2. Model Experimentation & Comparative Analysis

To satisfy rigorous academic benchmarking, five diverse supervised learning architectures were trained on the candidate dataset (1.15 million candidate arc instances across 80 training trips). To prevent severe data leakage from sequential GPS autocorrelation, 5-Fold GroupKFold cross-validation grouped strictly by trip_id was enforced.

Figure 2: Multi-metric comparison across the 5 architectures evaluating CV Log Loss, Top-1 Point Accuracy, and Training/Inference Speed.

Architectural Decision: While all four tree-based models achieved comparable log loss (~0.158–0.174), CatBoost and LightGBM dominated computational efficiency. CatBoost was chosen as the primary production scorer due to its best-in-class log-loss calibration (0.1585) and ultra-fast C++ inference speed (0.25ms/1k candidates). LightGBM delivered the fastest training convergence (0.16s), making it ideal for continuous pipeline retraining. RBF SVM exhibited severe scalability bottlenecks (180ms/1k latency and 42s training time), making it impractical for high-throughput map-matching.

3. Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimization

Hyperparameters were systematically optimized using Optuna's Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) over 20 iterations. The objective function minimized out-of-fold GroupKFold log-loss to maintain calibrated posterior candidate probabilities.

4. Distance-Aware Hidden Markov Model & Viterbi Decoding

Independent pointwise classification produces physically disjoint predictions when GPS drift fluctuates. To enforce topological road connectivity, we implemented a Distance-Aware HMM with dynamic Viterbi decoding.

δt(j) = maxi [ δt-1(i) · P(arcj | arci) ] · P(obst | arcj)

Probabilistic Modeling

  • Emission Probability P(obst | arcj): Modeled directly from the calibrated ML candidate probability, normalized over active candidate arcs: P(obst | arcj) = PML(arcj) / ∑k PML(arck).
  • Transition Probability P(arcj | arci): Penalizes transitions that violate road network topology:
    • If target_node(arci) == source_node(arcj) (direct graph connection): Ptrans = 1.0.
    • If arci == arcj (vehicle remains on same segment): Ptrans = 0.95.
    • If disconnected: penalized exponentially by the Euclidean gap between target_node(arci) and source_node(arcj) using decay factor β = 50.0m: Ptrans = 0.05 · exp(-dist / β).
  • Temporal Gap Handling: When Δt > 2s occurs, the transition penalty relaxes dynamically proportional to elapsed time, preventing false penalties during sensor packet drops.

6. Distributed 2-Laptop Deployment & API Verification

PathSnap was deployed across two physical machines adhering strictly to Section 6 of the hackathon evaluation guidelines:

  • Laptop 1 (Inference Server): Hosts FastAPI (src/pathsnap/service/api.py) running on port 8000. Houses all model weights, road subgraphs, and ground-truth validation routes. Exposes formatted terminal logging for evaluator oversight.
  • Laptop 2 (Evaluator Console): Runs Streamlit UI (src/pathsnap/ui/app.py). Communicates with Laptop 1 via local Wi-Fi, triggers evaluation runs, receives metric payloads, and renders interactive Folium maps with layer controls.
